title: Level, slope and curvature
objectives: Run PCA on yield curve changes in NumPy and name the factors.
Sort `eigh` output and fix eigenvector signs.
Use the first components to describe and hedge curve risk.

screens.title: Fifteen days of the curve
screens.prose: Each bar is the day's change in one gilt yield, from 2 years to 30 years, in basis points. Slide through the fifteen days.

derive.caption: Day {{d}} of 15: changes in basis points

screens.question: On how many of the 15 days do all five yields move in the same direction?

hints.text: A day counts when every bar is above zero, or every bar is below.
Day 1 counts: all five bars are below zero.
Only days 4, 8, 14 and 15 have bars on both sides of zero. That leaves 11.

feedback.correct: Most days the whole curve shifts one way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step through each day and count those with every bar on one side of zero.

byKey.few: You may have counted only big moves. Small days count too, if all five bars share a sign.
byKey.all: Days 4, 8, 14 and 15 have bars on both sides of zero. Day 15 steepens: short yields up, long yields down.

explain.text: On 11 of 15 days the whole curve moved one way. Day 15 is different: the short end rose and the long end fell. PCA will separate those two kinds of move.

screens.title: Covariance and eigh
screens.prose: The matrix `X` holds the 15 days, one column per maturity. Complete `pca_eigen` so it returns the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, largest first, with matching eigenvector columns. `np.linalg.eigh` handles symmetric matrices but returns the smallest eigenvalue first.
screens.question: Complete `pca_eigen(X)`.

tests.call: all(a >= b for a, b in zip(v, v[1:]))

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests on `X` and on a second data set. Each value is rounded to 4 decimal places and must match, a tolerance of 0.00005. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Demean with `X.mean(axis=0)`; it gives one mean per column.
`np.argsort(vals)` lists positions smallest first. Reverse it with `[::-1]`.
`Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)`, `C = Xc.T @ Xc / (len(X) - 1)`, `order = np.argsort(vals)[::-1]`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the demeaning, the $n - 1$ and the order.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace all three `...` lines.

explain.text:
The covariance is $\mathbf{X}_c^T\mathbf{X}_c/(n-1)$ after demeaning each column. `eigh` returns ascending eigenvalues, so the order is reversed.

```python
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
C = Xc.T @ Xc / (len(X) - 1)
order = np.argsort(vals)[::-1]
```

screens.title: Share of the variance
screens.prose: The total variance is the sum of the eigenvalues. Each component's share is its eigenvalue over that total. `pca_eigen` from the last screen is already in place.
screens.question: Complete `explained(X)` so it returns each component's share, largest first.

widget.how: Check runs 4 hidden tests. Values are rounded to 4 decimal places and must match, a tolerance of 0.00005.

hints.text: A share is one eigenvalue divided by all of them added up.
`vals.sum()` is the total variance.
`return vals / vals.sum()`

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Divide every eigenvalue by their sum.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace the `...` with an expression.

explain.text: `vals / vals.sum()` divides every eigenvalue by the trace. The first component carries 80.7% of the daily variance, the first two 96.7%. Five yields really move with about two or three degrees of freedom.

screens.title: Which end is PC1
screens.prose:
A colleague skips the sorting step:

```python
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(C)
pc1 = vecs[:, 0]
```

The table shows the `vals` that `eigh` returned for our yield data.
screens.question: What is the colleague's `pc1`?

options.text: The component with the smallest variance, 0.0235

options.why: `eigh` sorts eigenvalues from smallest to largest. Column 0 is the least important component, not the most.

options.text: An arbitrary component: the order is not defined
options.why: That is true of `np.linalg.eig`, not `eigh`. `eigh` always returns ascending order, so column 0 is the smallest.
Signs can flip, but the order here is wrong too. Column 0 belongs to eigenvalue 0.0235.

hints.text: Read the eigenvalue in position 0.
Position 0 holds the smallest eigenvalue.
`vecs[:, 0]` goes with 0.0235, which explains 0.05% of the variance. PC1 is `vecs[:, -1]`.

feedback.correct: Column 0 of `eigh` is the smallest component.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at which eigenvalue sits in position 0.

byKey.level: You assumed `eigh` sorts largest first. It sorts smallest first, so column 0 is noise.

explain.text: `eigh` returns ascending eigenvalues, so PC1 is the last column. `np.linalg.eig` is worse on a covariance matrix: it promises no order and may return a complex array with `+0j` parts. Use `eigh` and sort descending.

screens.title: Fix the signs
screens.prose: An eigenvector and its negative are equally valid, so a library may return either. To make loadings repeatable, flip each column so its largest-magnitude entry is positive.
screens.question: Complete `loadings(X, k)` so it returns the first `k` components, one per column, with that sign rule.

tests.call: all(L[np.argmax(np.abs(L[:, j])), j] > 0 for j in range(3))

widget.how: Check runs 4 hidden tests. Loadings are rounded to 4 decimal places and must match, a tolerance of 0.00005.

hints.text: `np.abs(L[:, j])` gives the sizes in column j.
`np.argmax` returns the position of the largest one.
`i = np.argmax(np.abs(L[:, j]))`, then `L[:, j] = -L[:, j]` when `L[i, j] < 0`.

feedback.correct: Every column now has a fixed sign.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Find the largest |loading| in each column and make it positive.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace both `...` lines.

explain.text:
Flipping a whole column changes nothing about the component, only how it is reported. A fixed rule makes results comparable across days and libraries.

```python
i = np.argmax(np.abs(L[:, j]))
if L[i, j] < 0:
    L[:, j] = -L[:, j]
```

screens.title: Level, slope, curvature
screens.prose: The bars are the loadings your function returned. Slide between the first three components. Count how often each one changes sign along the curve.
screens.question: Name each component.

hints.text: Count the sign changes from 2y to 30y in each component.
PC2 is negative at the short end and positive at the long end.
PC1 has no sign change, PC2 one, PC3 two.

feedback.correct: Level, slope, curvature: 81%, 16% and 3% of the variance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to each component and count the sign changes.

explain.text: PC1 moves every yield the same way: a parallel shift. PC2 lifts the long end against the short end: steepening. PC3 bends the middle against both ends.

screens.prose: Another library, run on the same data, reports PC1 with every loading negative.
screens.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: Nothing new: it is the same level component with the opposite sign
This factor is about yields falling, not rising
options.why: A component is a direction for both rises and falls. Its scores flip sign with it, so the product is unchanged.

options.text: One of the libraries has a bug
options.why: Both answers are correct. $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ holds for $-\mathbf{v}$ too.

hints.text: Is $-\mathbf{v}$ an eigenvector when $\mathbf{v}$ is?
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(-\mathbf{v}) = \lambda(-\mathbf{v})$.
Flip every bar and you get your PC1. Scores flip too, so each day's fitted move is the same.

feedback.correct: Same component; the sign is a convention.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether $-\mathbf{v}$ satisfies the eigenvector equation.

explain.text: Your sign rule makes the largest loading positive, so you would flip this to match. That is the edge case PCA always has: a component is a line, not an arrow. Fix the sign before comparing loadings across runs.

screens.prose:
The pipeline you wrote computes $$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^T, \qquad \text{share}_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_j \lambda_j}$$ with the eigenvalues sorted largest first:

```python
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
C = Xc.T @ Xc / (len(X) - 1)
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(C)
order = np.argsort(vals)[::-1]
```
screens.question: What share of the variance do level and slope explain together?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the shares of PC1 and PC2.

byKey.one: That is PC1 alone. Add PC2's 16.0%.

explain.text: Two numbers a day describe 96.7% of how five yields move. That is why desks quote curve risk as level and slope.

screens.title: Hedging a bond book
screens.prose: A gilt book loses money when yields rise. Its sensitivity column is the P&L in £ for a 1 bp rise at each maturity. A move of one unit of PC1 raises each yield by its loading, in bp.
screens.question: What is the book's P&L, in £, for a one-unit PC1 move?

hints.text: P&L is each sensitivity times that yield's move, added up.
The 10y moves 0.44 bp and costs £300 per bp.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each sensitivity by its PC1 loading and add.

byKey.sum: −£900 assumes every yield rises a full 1 bp. A unit of PC1 moves each yield by its loading, under 0.5 bp.
byKey.sign: Yields rise in a positive PC1 move, and this book loses when yields rise.

explain.text: The book's PC1 exposure is −£399 per unit, and its PC2 exposure is +£63. Two hedges, say 2y and 30y futures, can set both to zero. What is left is exposed to PCs 3 to 5: 3.3% of the variance, instead of five yields to hedge one by one.

ideas: Demean, form the covariance, `eigh`, then sort descending: the columns are the principal components.
On yield curve changes the first three are level (no sign change), slope (one) and curvature (two).
Two or three components explain almost all the variance. Hedge a book against them, not against five yields.
summary.trap: `eigh` returns the smallest eigenvalue first, and `eig` promises no order: sort before you read PC1.

quiz.prose: `vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(C)` on a covariance matrix `C`.
quiz.question: Which expression is PC1?

options.why: `eigh` sorts ascending, so column 0 has the smallest eigenvalue.
That is the last row. Eigenvectors are the columns of `vecs`.

feedback.correct: The last column has the largest eigenvalue.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `eigh` sorts ascending, and eigenvectors are columns.

explain.text: `eigh` returns eigenvalues smallest first, with eigenvectors as columns. So `vecs[:, -1]` belongs to the largest eigenvalue.

quiz.prose: A component has loadings $(0.55, -0.10, -0.60, -0.20, 0.50)$ on the 2y, 5y, 10y, 20y and 30y yields.
quiz.question: Which name fits it?

options.why: Level has every loading the same sign. This one has both signs.
Slope changes sign once. This one changes sign twice, from 2y to 5y and from 20y to 30y.

feedback.correct: Two sign changes: the ends against the middle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the sign changes from 2y to 30y.

explain.text: The signs run $+, -, -, -, +$: the ends move against the belly. That is curvature.

quiz.prose: The eigenvalues of a yield-change covariance matrix are 40, 8, 1.5, 0.4 and 0.1.
quiz.question: What share of the variance do the first two components explain?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the first two eigenvalues and divide by the total.

explain.text: The total is $40 + 8 + 1.5 + 0.4 + 0.1 = 50$. Level and slope carry 48 of it.

quiz.prose: A component comes back as $(-0.20, 0.30, -0.93)$. Your rule makes the largest-magnitude loading positive.
quiz.question: What do you report?

options.why: The largest magnitude is 0.93, and it is negative. The rule flips the column.
You took absolute values. That changes the direction; flip every sign together instead.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the largest |loading|; if it is negative, flip every sign.

explain.text: $|-0.93|$ is the largest, and it is negative, so multiply the whole vector by $-1$. Flipping every sign keeps the same component.
